newsitem.title: USA: Wisconsin looks to expand investor base for bonds.
newsitem.headline: Wisconsin looks to expand investor base for bonds.

text.p: Wisconsin is considering an idea to expand the institutional investor base for its bonds by offering underwriters a monetary incentive for selling bonds to new investors, a state official said Friday.
Frank Hoadley, Wisconsin's capital finance director, said an analysis of bondholders showed a "disturbing trend" that most of the state's debt is owned by a handful of institutional investors.

For example, 14 institutions currently own half of the state's $3.3 billion of outstanding general obligation debt, with one investor owning 25 percent of the debt, Hoadley said. While the total universe of institutional investors stands at about 9,000, he said only 250 hold Wisconsin bonds.

He said this concentration leads to thin books on bond sale days, where one investor's priority order may end up circumventing a repricing of a deal and a chance at lowering yields in oversubscribed maturities.
More investors, on the other hand, would thicken the book and lead to more competition in the market for Wisconsin paper, he added.

Hoadley's idea is to set up a per-bond pot of money called an incentive management fee that would be available to underwriters of a negotiated deal who bring in new investors. The state would set a goal of new investors for the deal and would reward underwriters with money from the pot for their efforts.

"We are going to have an incentive pot and the purpose of the pot is to encourage syndicate members to go out and call on specific investors who have not bought the state's bonds before," Hoadley said.
He added that the idea has not been tried before.
Hoadley said the idea of monetary incentive for bringing in new investors arose with a $75 million clean water revenue bond issue the state sold last month.
He said underwriters were at first skeptical of the idea then became "enthusiastic."
"We ran out of time," Hoadley said, explaining why the idea was not incorporated into the deal. "The idea required some fairly extensive discussion with each member in the group."
Hoadley said an incentive management fee may be considered for a future negotiated issue.
